lead: A missile rarely flies straight at its target. It must hold a stable roll attitude, turn a guidance command into sideways acceleration, and sometimes roll its whole body so its lift points the right way. The roll autopilot holds the airframe about its long axis. The lateral autopilot turns an acceleration demand into fin motion. Bank-to-turn guidance combines them: roll to a computed bank angle, then pull. These loops sit between the guidance law and the fins, and they decide whether a hit is smooth or wasted.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.6 for the airframe and fin servos, and Unit 1 for autopilot basics.

sections.h3: Roll autopilot: hold the long axis

blocks.text: The roll autopilot controls rotation about the missile's long axis. The controlled variable is roll angle φ, measured from a reference such as wings level. Its derivative is roll rate p = dφ/dt. A rate gyro measures p. A free or vertical gyro, or an attitude reference, measures φ. The autopilot forms a command from the attitude error and adds roll-rate damping.

blocks.where: δ<sub>a</sub> is the aileron or roll-fin deflection, in radians; φ is the measured roll angle, in radians; φ<sub>cmd</sub> is the commanded roll angle, in radians; p is roll rate, in radians per second; K<sub>φ</sub> is the attitude gain, in radians of fin per radian of roll error; K<sub>p</sub> is the rate gain, in radians of fin per radian per second.

blocks.text: The negative sign on K<sub>p</sub> opposes roll rate. Without it, the missile overshoots the commanded bank. Wings-level mode is φ<sub>cmd</sub> = 0. Gain scheduling with Mach and altitude keeps the loop response similar as dynamic pressure changes. Modern missiles use ring laser or fibre optic gyros, which have no spinning mass and low drift; dynamically tuned gyros, which do have a small spinning rotor, are also used. The roll loop must be faster than the lateral loop, so bank angle is ready before lift is applied.

The lateral autopilot converts a guidance acceleration command into yaw motion. Its outer loop uses an accelerometer to measure lateral acceleration a<sub>y</sub>. The error is e = a<sub>cmd</sub> − a<sub>y</sub>, where a<sub>cmd</sub> is the commanded lateral acceleration and a<sub>y</sub> is the measured value, both in m/s². The outer loop turns e into a yaw-rate command r<sub>cmd</sub>; an integral term removes steady error. The inner loop uses a yaw rate gyro. It compares r with r<sub>cmd</sub> and commands the rudder or yaw fins. A simple inner law is δ<sub>r</sub> = K<sub>r</sub>(r<sub>cmd</sub> − r). δ<sub>r</sub> is rudder deflection in radians, K<sub>r</sub> is the rate gain, and r is measured yaw rate in rad/s. Rate feedback damps the short-period yaw oscillation.

Gains are scheduled with Mach and altitude. At low dynamic pressure the fins are weak and need larger deflection for the same acceleration. At high dynamic pressure the same deflection gives more acceleration, so gains fall. The accelerometer and rate gyro are the transducers described in Unit 4. In a skid-to-turn missile this loop works with pitch and yaw without rolling. In a bank-to-turn missile the same acceleration demand is split: the roll autopilot sets the lift direction, and the in-plane loop sets angle of attack.

Bank-to-turn guidance uses one lift plane. The guidance law produces a commanded acceleration vector. Let a<sub>total</sub> be its magnitude. Before rolling, the vector has an in-plane part a<sub>in</sub> = a<sub>total</sub> cos φ and a sideways part a<sub>side</sub> = a<sub>total</sub> sin φ, where φ is the required bank angle. The roll autopilot rolls the airframe by φ until the lift plane contains the commanded vector. The roll puts both parts into the lift plane, so the wing must give lift a<sub>L</sub> = a<sub>total</sub>. The turn itself comes from angle of attack, not from the roll. Roll only points the lift vector.
sin φ = a<sub>side</sub> ÷ a<sub>total</sub>; a<sub>in</sub> = a<sub>total</sub> cos φ; a<sub>L</sub> = a<sub>total</sub>
blocks.where: φ is the required bank angle, in radians; a<sub>total</sub> is the magnitude of the commanded acceleration, in m/s²; a<sub>side</sub> is the component normal to the current lift plane, in m/s²; a<sub>in</sub> is the in-plane component before rolling, in m/s²; a<sub>L</sub> is the lift acceleration required after rolling, equal to a<sub>total</sub>, in m/s².

items: Take the guidance acceleration vector; find its magnitude a<sub>total</sub> and the component a<sub>side</sub> normal to the current lift plane.
Compute the bank command φ = asin(a<sub>side</sub> ÷ a<sub>total</sub>).
Roll the airframe with the roll autopilot until φ is reached and settled.
Command angle of attack so the lift in the body plane equals a<sub>total</sub>.

blocks.text: Compare with skid-to-turn. STT keeps the airframe unrolled and uses separate pitch and yaw fins. It reverses direction quickly and avoids roll cross-coupling. It uses two lifting planes and usually more drag. BTT uses one lifting surface, so it can have less trim drag and longer range. It needs a high roll rate to move the lift plane, suffers inertia cross-coupling between roll and yaw, and reverses a turn slowly because the body must roll first. The roll loop bandwidth must sit well above the lateral loop, otherwise the lift vector is not steady when the pull starts.

spec.title: Roll autopilot loop
spec.aria: Roll loop: the roll command enters the autopilot, the fins roll the missile, and a rate gyro feeds roll rate back to the autopilot.

examples.question: A bank-to-turn missile must accelerate at 8 g in a direction that lies 4 g to the side of its lift plane. Find the bank angle and the lift the wing must give.
steps: Given: a<sub>total</sub> = 8 g, a<sub>side</sub> = 4 g. g is the acceleration due to gravity, 9.81 m/s², so 8 g = 78.5 m/s².

Lift after the roll: a<sub>L</sub> = a<sub>total</sub> = 8 g = 78.5 m/s². Before rolling, the in-plane component was a<sub>in</sub> = a<sub>total</sub> cos φ = 8 × cos 30° = 8 × 0.8660 = 6.928 g, about 6.93 g.
The roll autopilot must settle at 30° before the lateral autopilot pulls the full 8 g of lift.
examples.answer: The bank angle is 30.0° and the wing must give 8 g of lift, about 78.5 m/s².
examples.check:
import math

a_total = 8.0
a_side = 4.0
phi_deg = math.degrees(math.asin(a_side / a_total))
lift_g = a_total
inplane_g = a_total * math.cos(math.radians(phi_deg))
print(round(phi_deg, 1))
print(round(lift_g, 2))

traps: Roll alone does not turn a BTT missile. The turn comes from the angle of attack applied after the roll; roll only aims the lift vector.
Do not use a_L = a_total sin φ. After the roll the lift is the full command a_total; its components along the old lift plane and across it are a_total cos φ and a_total sin φ.
The roll loop must be faster than the lateral loop. If both have similar bandwidth, the lift vector moves while the missile is pulling.
BTT is not automatically better. It saves drag with one lifting plane but needs high roll rate and suffers inertia cross-coupling; STT reverses faster.
Bank angle sign matters: φ must point the lift toward the commanded acceleration, not away from it.

quiz.q: What does a roll autopilot control?
quiz.a: It controls rotation about the missile's long axis, holding roll angle or wings level.

quiz.q: Why is roll rate fed back in the roll loop?
quiz.a: Rate feedback opposes fast roll motion and adds damping, so the missile does not overshoot the commanded bank angle.

quiz.q: A BTT missile needs a<sub>total</sub> = 6 g and a<sub>side</sub> = 3 g. Find the bank angle and the lift the wing must give.
quiz.a: sin φ = 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5, so φ = 30.0°. After the roll the lift is a_L = a_total = 6 g; the in-plane component before rolling was 6 cos 30° = 5.196 g, about 5.20 g.

quiz.q: Explain why a BTT missile may reverse a turn more slowly than an STT missile.
quiz.a: BTT must first roll the whole body to move its single lift plane, then change angle of attack. STT can command the opposite yaw or pitch directly, so it reverses without waiting for a roll.

quiz.q: Name two sensors used in a lateral autopilot and state what each measures.
quiz.a: An accelerometer measures lateral acceleration; a rate gyro measures yaw rate.

quiz.q: Why are autopilot gains scheduled with Mach and altitude?
quiz.a: Fin effectiveness depends on dynamic pressure, which changes with speed and altitude. Scheduling keeps the loop response similar across the flight envelope.

quiz.q: A roll loop has bandwidth close to the lateral loop bandwidth. What problem follows?
quiz.a: The bank angle may still be moving when the lateral loop applies angle of attack. The lift vector then points in a changing direction, causing cross-coupling and poor turn accuracy.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern BTT designs use high roll-rate autopilots and gain-scheduled roll and yaw loops to manage inertia cross-coupling. Fibre optic gyros and digital signal processing make the roll loop fast and quiet. Search for bank-to-turn autopilot design, roll-yaw cross-coupling, and skid-to-turn versus bank-to-turn.
